question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

The ______ mistake these couples made was not spending enough time seriously planning for a lifetime together in marriage.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. egregious.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Egregious means outstandingly bad, shocking or glaring — it collocates naturally with words like *mistake*, *error*, *blunder*, *lie*. (घोर, अत्यंत बुरा)

◦ The sentence describes a serious failure — not planning for a lifetime together — so an adjective meaning ‘very bad/glaring’ is required.

◦ Correct: The egregious mistake these couples made was not spending enough time seriously planning for a lifetime together in marriage.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Sporadic – occurring at irregular intervals, scattered (छिटपुट); a mistake is not ‘sporadic’ here.

• Credulous – too ready to believe things, gullible (भोला/विश्वासी); describes a person, not a mistake.

• Enigmatic – mysterious, puzzling (रहस्यमय); it does not convey the idea of seriousness of the error.

NOTE

• Common collocations: *egregious error/blunder*, *sporadic violence/rainfall*, *credulous investor*, *enigmatic smile*.

• Synonyms of egregious: flagrant, blatant, glaring, outrageous.

question:
Select the word segment that substitutes (replaces) the bracketed word segment correctly and completes the sentence meaningfully. Select the option 'no correction required' if the sentence is correct as given.

(They was standing) at one end of a very long and splendid hall.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. They were standing.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The subject They is plural, so the plural past form of ‘be’ — were — must be used, not the singular ‘was’. (कर्ता-क्रिया मेल)

◦ The action is a continuous state in the past, so the Past Continuous structure *was/were + V1+ing* is needed: were standing.

◦ Correct: They were standing at one end of a very long and splendid hall.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2 is wrong because ‘They was’ is a clear subject-verb agreement error.

• Option 3 ‘were standed’ is wrong — stand is an irregular verb (stand – stood – stood); ‘standed’ does not exist.

• Option 4 ‘had been standed’ repeats the same non-existent form and also gives the wrong tense.

NOTE

• Irregular verbs often tested: stand–stood–stood, understand–understood–understood, withstand–withstood–withstood.

• Rule: I/he/she/it + was; we/you/they + were.

question:
Select the most appropriate antonym of the given word.

Topple
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Steady.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Topple means to fall over or to overthrow/bring down (a government, a ruler). (गिराना, लुढ़कना)

◦ Steady means firm, stable, not shaking or falling — the exact opposite of toppling. (स्थिर)

◦ Correct: The statue began to topple, so two workers rushed to steady it.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Fumble – to handle clumsily or grope about (टटोलना); not an antonym.

• Tumble – to fall suddenly (लुढ़कना); this is a synonym of topple, not an antonym.

• Plunge – to fall or dive steeply downwards (गोता लगाना); again close in sense to falling.

NOTE

• Synonyms of topple: overturn, overthrow, unseat, capsize, tumble.

• Antonyms of topple: steady, stabilise, uphold, support, erect.

question: Four sentences are given, out of which three have spelling errors. Choose the sentence with all correctly spelt words.
option_1: It is demonstrably an unfair comparsion.
option_2: There is a room at the extreme end of the corridor.
option_3: The whole thing is foriegn to us.
option_4: I'm the sole victim of Mother's tyrany.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. There is a room at the extreme end of the corridor.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Every word in Option 2 — *extreme*, *end*, *corridor* — is spelt correctly, so it is the only error-free sentence. (गलियारा)

◦ Note the double ‘r’ in corridor (co-rri-dor) — a very commonly misspelt SSC word.

◦ Correct: There is a room at the extreme end of the corridor.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: “comparsion” is wrong; the correct spelling is comparison.

• Option 3: “foriegn” is wrong; the correct spelling is foreign (‘e’ before ‘i’ here — an exception to ‘i before e’).

• Option 4: “tyrany” is wrong; the correct spelling is tyranny (double ‘n’).

NOTE

• Frequently misspelt pairs: occurrence, embarrass, harass, committee, maintenance, privilege, definitely.

• ‘i before e except after c’ fails for: foreign, seize, weird, height, neither, leisure.

question:
Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error. If there is no error, select 'No error'.

The baby's faces are expressionless and/ their pupils aren't visible which gives/ the appearance of lifelessness and dreadfulness.
option_2: the appearance of lifelessness and dreadfulness.
option_3: their pupils aren't visible which gives
option_4: The baby's faces are expressionless and
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. The baby's faces are expressionless and.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• A single baby has only one face, so the plural noun ‘faces’ is wrong; it must be the singular face, and the verb then becomes is. (एकवचन)

◦ The following segments refer to ‘their pupils’ (the babies’ eyes), so the intended reading is the plural babies' faces are; either way the printed segment ‘The baby's faces are’ is faulty.

◦ Correct: The babies' faces are expressionless and their pupils aren't visible, which gives the appearance of lifelessness and dreadfulness.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 2 ‘the appearance of lifelessness and dreadfulness’ is grammatically sound.

• Option 3 ‘their pupils aren’t visible which gives’ is acceptable in this segmented sentence.

• Option 1 ‘No error’ is wrong because the first segment does contain the number/agreement mistake.

NOTE

• Possessives: singular → baby's; plural → babies'; the apostrophe shifts after the plural ‘-s’.

• Similar: child's / children's, man's / men's, lady's / ladies'.

question:
Find the part of the given sentence that has an error in it. If there is no error, choose ‘No error’.

I don’t want to get involved in these game of gambling.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. these game of gambling.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• These is a plural demonstrative and cannot modify the singular noun game; the singular demonstrative this is required. (संकेतवाचक सर्वनाम)

◦ Demonstrative adjectives must agree in number with the noun: *this/that* + singular, *these/those* + plural.

◦ Correct: I don’t want to get involved in this game of gambling.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 ‘get involved in’ is correct — the fixed preposition after *involved* is in.

• Option 4 ‘I don’t want to’ is correct — *want* is followed by a to-infinitive.

• Option 2 ‘No error’ is wrong because the third segment carries the number error.

NOTE

• this/that + singular noun; these/those + plural noun. E.g., *this book*, *these books*.

• Fixed prepositions: involved in, interested in, engaged in, indulge in.

question:
Select the word segment that substitutes (replaces) the bracketed word segment correctly and completes the sentence meaningfully. Select the option 'no correction required' if the sentence is correct as given.

Both of us felt the relationship (wasn't really gone somewhere.)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. wasn't really going anywhere.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom ‘go anywhere’ (usually negative — *not going anywhere*) means to make no progress; it is the natural expression for a stagnant relationship. (आगे न बढ़ना)

◦ In a negative sentence anywhere is used, not ‘somewhere’; and the past continuous was going is needed after ‘wasn't’, not the past participle ‘gone’.

◦ Correct: Both of us felt the relationship wasn't really going anywhere.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1 ‘won’t really gone that path’ mixes a future contraction with a past participle — doubly ungrammatical.

• Option 2 ‘was going that direction’ needs the preposition in (*in that direction*) and loses the intended negative sense.

• Option 3 is wrong because the bracketed part ‘wasn't really gone somewhere’ is ungrammatical as printed.

NOTE

• Some/any rule: some in affirmatives, any/anywhere/anything in negatives and questions.

• Related idioms: *not going anywhere* (making no progress), *go places* (to succeed).

question: Choose the incorrectly spelt word.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Conssume.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct spelling is consume — with a single ‘s’; the printed ‘Conssume’ wrongly doubles the ‘s’. (उपभोग करना)

◦ Consume means to eat, drink or use up. Related forms: *consumer*, *consumption*, *consumable*.

◦ Correct: Indians consume more tea than coffee.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Horror – correctly spelt; a feeling of intense fear or shock (डर).

• Showing – correctly spelt; ‘show’ + ‘-ing’ with no letter change.

• Motive – correctly spelt; a reason for doing something (उद्देश्य).

NOTE

• Words often wrongly doubled: *always* (not allways), *until* (not untill), *recommend* (double ‘m’, single ‘c’).

• Note the spelling change: consume → consumption (the ‘e’ is dropped and ‘pt’ added).

question:
Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error. If there is no error, select 'No error'.

Two border guards patrolling / the nearby frontier with Georgia have also / been reported missing from Friday night.
option_1: the nearby frontier with Georgia have also
option_2: been reported missing from Friday night.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. been reported missing from Friday night.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• With a point of time in the perfect tense we use since, not ‘from’: *since Friday night*. (समय-बिंदु के लिए 'since')

◦ ‘From’ needs a stated end point (*from Monday to Friday*), whereas since links a past point to the present, which suits ‘have been reported’.

◦ Correct: Two border guards patrolling the nearby frontier with Georgia have also been reported missing since Friday night.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1 is correct — the plural subject ‘Two border guards’ takes the plural auxiliary have.

• Option 3 is correct — ‘patrolling’ is a participle phrase modifying ‘guards’.

• Option 4 ‘No Error’ is wrong because the preposition mistake is present.

NOTE

• since + point of time (since 2010, since Monday); for + period of time (for two years).

• Present Perfect Continuous is generally used with since/for: *He has been living here since 2015*.

question:
Select the appropriate synonym for the underlined word.

It can be easy to ignore people who are struggling and having a hard time.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. hustling.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Struggling means making great effort against difficulty — the sentence itself adds ‘having a hard time’. (संघर्ष करना)

◦ Hustling means working or pushing hard, hurrying and striving — the closest match among the options. (जी-तोड़ मेहनत करना)

◦ Correct: It can be easy to ignore people who are hustling and having a hard time.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Claiming – asserting a right or stating something as true (दावा करना); unrelated to hardship.

• Gliding – moving smoothly and effortlessly (सरकना); it is the opposite idea of struggling.

• Booming – flourishing, growing rapidly (तेजी पर होना); again opposite in sense.

NOTE

• Synonyms of struggle: strive, grapple, toil, wrestle, labour.

• Antonyms of struggle: glide, coast, breeze through, flourish.

question:
A sentence has been given with a blank to be filled with an appropriate option. Choose the correct alternative.

The survival of theatre has depended on the creation of ______ formats.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. new.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank qualifies the plural noun formats, so an adjective in the positive degree is needed — new. (विशेषण)

◦ No comparison is being made in the sentence, so the comparative or superlative degree is not justified.

◦ Correct: The survival of theatre has depended on the creation of new formats.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Newly is an adverb (*newly built house*) and cannot directly modify a noun.

• Newer is comparative and needs a ‘than’ comparison or a clear second item.

• Newest is superlative and normally requires the before it (*the newest formats*).

NOTE

• Degrees: new – newer – newest; the superlative almost always takes the.

• Adjective modifies a noun; adverb modifies a verb, adjective or another adverb.

question:
In the following question, out of the given four alternatives, select the alternative which best expresses the meaning of the Idiom/Phrase.

To get under one’s skin
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. To anger or irritate.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom ‘to get under one’s skin’ means to irritate or annoy someone deeply. (किसी को चिढ़ाना/खीझाना)

◦ It can also mean to affect someone intensely, but in SSC exams the standard tested sense is to annoy/irritate.

◦ Correct: His constant boasting really gets under my skin.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• ‘To get nowhere’ means to make no progress — a different idiom altogether.

• ‘To hide something’ matches idioms like *sweep under the carpet*, not this one.

• ‘To behave foolishly’ matches *play the fool*, not *get under one’s skin*.

NOTE

• Similar idioms of annoyance: *rub someone the wrong way*, *drive someone up the wall*, *get on one’s nerves*.

• Other ‘skin’ idioms: *save one’s skin* (escape danger), *by the skin of one’s teeth* (very narrowly).

question:
Choose the word that means the same as the given word.

Gala
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Carnival.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• A gala is a festive occasion or grand celebration/social event. (उत्सव, समारोह)

◦ A carnival is likewise a public festival with merry-making — the closest synonym here. (मेला/उत्सव)

◦ Correct: The school hosted a gala (a carnival) to mark its golden jubilee.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Mistakenly – by mistake, in error (गलती से); an adverb, unrelated to celebration.

• Funeral – the ceremony of burying or cremating the dead (अंत्येष्टि); an occasion of mourning, the very opposite mood.

• Moist – slightly wet (नम); an adjective describing dampness.

NOTE

• Synonyms of gala: festival, fete, jamboree, revelry, celebration.

• ‘Gala’ also works as an adjective: *a gala night*, *a gala dinner*.

question:
Fill in the blank with the most appropriate option.

He is quite ______ and narrow.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. tall.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The pronoun He refers to a person, and a person’s vertical measurement is described by tall, never by ‘long’. (लंबा कद)

◦ ‘Tall and narrow’ is the natural pairing to describe a thin, high build.

◦ Correct: He is quite tall and narrow.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Long is used for horizontal extent or duration (*a long road*, *a long speech*), not for a person’s height.

• Stretched means pulled out or extended by force — inappropriate for describing a person’s build.

• Elongated means made unnaturally long; it describes shapes or objects, not a person’s stature.

NOTE

• Height words: tall for people, trees, buildings; high for mountains, walls, prices.

• *How tall are you?* (person) vs *How high is the wall?* (object).

question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the bracketed idiom in the given sentence.

Critics and Monday morning quarterbacks are (a dime a dozen), but it remains to be seen.
option_1: Avoiding the main topic, not speaking directly about the issue
option_2: To force an issue that has already ended
option_3: Anything that is common and easy to get
option_4: Stuck between two very bad options
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Anything that is common and easy to get.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom ‘a dime a dozen’ means very common, plentiful and therefore of little value. (बहुत आम/सस्ता)

◦ The sentence says critics and armchair experts are everywhere — i.e., easily found and cheaply had.

◦ Correct: Critics and Monday morning quarterbacks are a dime a dozen, but it remains to be seen.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• ‘Avoiding the main topic’ is the meaning of *beat about the bush*.

• ‘To force an issue that has already ended’ corresponds to *flog a dead horse*.

• ‘Stuck between two very bad options’ is *between the devil and the deep blue sea* / *a Hobson’s choice* situation.

NOTE

• Money idioms: *a dime a dozen* (very common), *cost an arm and a leg* (very expensive), *worth its weight in gold* (very valuable).

• ‘Monday morning quarterback’ = one who criticises with hindsight after the event.

question:
Select the most appropriate word for the given group of words.

A small structure with one or more open sides that is used to vend merchandise
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Kiosk.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• A kiosk is a small open-fronted booth or cabin from which goods, tickets or information are sold. (गुमटी/खोखा)

◦ The definition’s key elements — *small structure*, *open sides*, *vend merchandise* — match ‘kiosk’ precisely.

◦ Correct: She bought a magazine from the newspaper kiosk at the station.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Stand is a general word for a raised platform or a stall; it is too vague to be the one-word substitute here.

• Vendor denotes a person who sells goods, not a structure.

• Podium is a small raised platform on which a speaker or conductor stands — nothing to do with selling.

NOTE

• Related one-word substitutes: stall (a small booth in a market), emporium (a large retail store), arcade (a covered walk with shops).

• Modern usage: an ATM kiosk or information kiosk — a self-service booth.

question:
Improve the underlined part of the sentence. Choose ‘No improvement’ as an answer if the sentence is grammatically correct.

When I was a kid, I used to pretend to be a knight in King Arthur's court.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. No improvement.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The structure ‘used to + V1 (bare infinitive)’ expresses a past habit that no longer continues — exactly what the sentence describes. (बीते समय की आदत)

◦ Here ‘used to pretend’ is perfectly formed, so no change is required.

◦ Correct: When I was a kid, I used to pretend to be a knight in King Arthur's court.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1 ‘used to pretending’ is wrong — the gerund follows only be/get used to (meaning ‘accustomed to’).

• Option 2 ‘used to pretends’ is wrong — an ‘-s’ form can never follow ‘used to’.

• Option 3 ‘use to pretend’ is wrong — in an affirmative sentence the past form used is required.

NOTE

• Contrast: *I used to swim* (past habit) vs *I am used to swimming* (accustomed to).

• In questions/negatives with ‘did’, the base form returns: *Did you use to live here?*

question:
Fill in the blank with the most appropriate option.

I have been on this project since the first day, hence I am responsible ______ it.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. for.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The fixed preposition after the adjective responsible, when referring to a thing or task one is answerable for, is for. (उत्तरदायी होना)

◦ ‘Responsible to’ is used only for the person/authority one reports to: *He is responsible to the manager*.

◦ Correct: I have been on this project since the first day, hence I am responsible for it.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• ‘Responsible from’ is not an English collocation at all.

• ‘Responsible to it’ is wrong because ‘it’ here is the project (a thing), not a superior.

• ‘Responsible by’ is likewise unidiomatic.

NOTE

• Adjective + preposition: responsible for, answerable for, accountable for, liable for, famous for.

• But: responsible to a boss, married to, similar to, addicted to.

question:
Select the appropriate antonym for the underlined word.

There is a point at which fear may turn to insanity.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Wisdom.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Insanity means madness — a state of unsoundness of mind or extreme foolishness. (पागलपन)

◦ Wisdom is sound judgement and good sense, the clear opposite of madness/folly. (बुद्धिमत्ता)

◦ Correct: There is a point at which fear may turn to insanity — only wisdom can hold it back.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Lunacy – madness, extreme folly (पागलपन); a synonym of insanity, not an antonym.

• Absurdity – ridiculousness, senselessness (बेतुकापन); again close in meaning to insanity.

• Frenzy – wild, uncontrolled excitement (उन्माद); also nearer to insanity than opposed to it.

NOTE

• Synonyms of insanity: lunacy, madness, dementia, derangement, folly.

• Antonyms of insanity: sanity, wisdom, prudence, rationality, sense.

question:
Select the most appropriate word for the given group of words.

Partial or total loss of memory
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Amnesia.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Amnesia is the partial or total loss of memory, usually caused by injury, shock or illness. (स्मृतिलोप)

◦ The word comes from Greek *a-* (without) + *mnesis* (memory).

◦ Correct: After the accident he suffered from amnesia and could not recall his own name.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Atheist – one who does not believe in the existence of God (नास्तिक).

• Ascetic – one who practises severe self-discipline and abstains from pleasures (तपस्वी).

• Axiom – a self-evident truth that needs no proof (स्वयंसिद्ध सत्य).

NOTE

• Related one-word substitutes: insomnia (inability to sleep), anaemia (deficiency of blood), amnesty (a general pardon).

• Belief words: theist, atheist, agnostic (one who says God is unknowable), heretic, apostate.

question:
In the following passage some of the words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the correct answer for the given blanks out of the four alternatives.

Alkaline hydrolysis is rare today as a funeral (1) ______ for humans. Offered to the public for the first time just over a (2) ______ ago, it is now permitted and regulated in 26 U.S. states, and practiced (3) ______ in North America, where it remains unfamiliar to most people who (4) ______ a loved one or who are thinking about what could (5) ______ to their own bodies when they die.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 1.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Practice.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank needs a noun that fits ‘a funeral ______ for humans’ — practice means a customary or established way of doing something. (प्रथा/रिवाज)

◦ The passage later says alkaline hydrolysis is ‘permitted and regulated’ and ‘practiced’, which confirms that it is being described as a funeral practice.

◦ Correct: Alkaline hydrolysis is rare today as a funeral practice for humans.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Proceeding usually refers to legal action or the record of a meeting — ‘funeral proceeding’ is unidiomatic.

• Activity is too general and does not convey an established custom.

• Judgement means a decision or opinion — completely out of context.

NOTE

• Collocations: *common practice*, *standard practice*, *religious practice*, *burial practice*.

• Note the spelling pair: practice (noun, British) vs practise (verb, British); American English uses *practice* for both.

question:
In the following passage some of the words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the correct answer for the given blanks out of the four alternatives.

Alkaline hydrolysis is rare today as a funeral (1) ______ for humans. Offered to the public for the first time just over a (2) ______ ago, it is now permitted and regulated in 26 U.S. states, and practiced (3) ______ in North America, where it remains unfamiliar to most people who (4) ______ a loved one or who are thinking about what could (5) ______ to their own bodies when they die.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 2.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. decade.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The phrase is ‘just over a (2) ______ ago’, which needs a definite unit of time preceded by ‘a’ — decade (ten years) fits exactly. (दशक)

◦ ‘Just over a decade ago’ is a standard English expression for slightly more than ten years back.

◦ Correct: Offered to the public for the first time just over a decade ago...

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Date would give ‘just over a date ago’, which is meaningless.

• Vintage refers to the year/harvest of wine or something of high quality from the past; it is not a measure of elapsed time.

• Period is vague — it names no fixed length, so ‘a period ago’ is unidiomatic.

NOTE

• Time units: decade = 10 years, score = 20 years, century = 100 years, millennium = 1000 years.

• Related words: *biennial* (every two years), *jubilee* (25/50 years).

question:
In the following passage some of the words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the correct answer for the given blanks out of the four alternatives.

Alkaline hydrolysis is rare today as a funeral (1) ______ for humans. Offered to the public for the first time just over a (2) ______ ago, it is now permitted and regulated in 26 U.S. states, and practiced (3) ______ in North America, where it remains unfamiliar to most people who (4) ______ a loved one or who are thinking about what could (5) ______ to their own bodies when they die.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 3.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. primarily.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank needs an adverb before ‘in North America’: primarily means mainly or chiefly. (मुख्य रूप से)

◦ The sentence contrasts limited legality in 26 U.S. states with the fact that the practice occurs chiefly in North America.

◦ Correct: ...and practiced primarily in North America, where it remains unfamiliar to most people.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Manly is an adjective meaning having qualities associated with men — grammatically and contextually wrong.

• Approximately means roughly and is used before numbers, not before a place name.

• Lastly introduces the final item in a list — there is no list here.

NOTE

• Synonyms of primarily: mainly, chiefly, principally, largely, predominantly.

• Adverbs ending in *-ly* modify verbs; adjectives such as *manly*, *friendly*, *lovely*, *costly* also end in *-ly* — do not confuse them.

question:
In the following passage some of the words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the correct answer for the given blanks out of the four alternatives.

Alkaline hydrolysis is rare today as a funeral (1) ______ for humans. Offered to the public for the first time just over a (2) ______ ago, it is now permitted and regulated in 26 U.S. states, and practiced (3) ______ in North America, where it remains unfamiliar to most people who (4) ______ a loved one or who are thinking about what could (5) ______ to their own bodies when they die.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 4.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. have lost.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The relative pronoun who refers to the plural antecedent most people, so the plural auxiliary have is required. (कर्ता-क्रिया मेल)

◦ The Present Perfect (*have lost*) shows a past bereavement whose effect continues into the present, matching the tense of ‘remains unfamiliar’.

◦ Correct: ...it remains unfamiliar to most people who have lost a loved one...

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• has lost is singular and does not agree with ‘people’.

• loose is an adjective meaning ‘not tight’ (ढीला) — a classic spelling trap, not a verb form here.

• lose (present tense) breaks the tense sequence; the loss is already complete.

NOTE

• lose (verb, to be deprived of) vs loose (adjective, not tight) vs loss (noun).

• ‘People’ is a plural noun and always takes a plural verb: *People are waiting*.

question:
In the following passage some of the words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the correct answer for the given blanks out of the four alternatives.

Alkaline hydrolysis is rare today as a funeral (1) ______ for humans. Offered to the public for the first time just over a (2) ______ ago, it is now permitted and regulated in 26 U.S. states, and practiced (3) ______ in North America, where it remains unfamiliar to most people who (4) ______ a loved one or who are thinking about what could (5) ______ to their own bodies when they die.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 5.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. happen.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The clause is ‘what could (5) ______ to their own bodies’, and the verb that idiomatically takes ‘to’ in this sense is happen. (घटित होना)

◦ *Happen to somebody/something* = to occur or befall; after the modal ‘could’ the bare infinitive happen is correct.

◦ Correct: ...who are thinking about what could happen to their own bodies when they die.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Syndicate means to sell (an article, etc.) to several outlets or to form a syndicate — out of context.

• Curtail means to cut short or reduce (घटाना); it takes a direct object, not ‘to’.

• Gravitate means to be drawn towards something (*gravitate towards*), which does not fit the meaning here.

NOTE

• Modal + bare infinitive: can/could/may/might/must/should + V1 (no ‘to’, no ‘-s’, no ‘-ing’).

• Verb + preposition: *happen to*, *occur to*, *belong to*, *refer to*, *gravitate towards*.
